title: Questions in the Temple: Authority, Caesar, and the Resurrection
summary: Teaching in the temple courts, Jesus is challenged by the chief priests, scribes, and elders about his authority, and he answers with a question about John's baptism and a parable of tenants who kill the vineyard owner's son. Spies ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, and Sadducees pose a riddle about marriage in the resurrection. Jesus silences both, asks his own question about how the Messiah can be David's son and Lord, and warns against the scribes' love of honor.
story: Jesus has entered Jerusalem as king and cleared the temple, and now he occupies it, teaching daily. The leaders who were plotting his death at the end of chapter 19 come at him with public questions designed to discredit him or hand him to the Roman governor. Luke arranges a series of controversies, one after another, in which Jesus' opponents are silenced and the people remain on his side. The parable of the tenants lays bare what is really happening: the leaders of Israel are about to reject and kill the owner's beloved son. By the end of the chapter no one dares to question him further, and the stage is set for his arrest.
historical:
The chief priests belonged to a small group of priestly families who controlled the temple and held power under Roman oversight. The high priest was appointed by the Roman governor, and the council (the Sanhedrin) combined chief priests, elders from leading families, and scribes, experts in the Law. The Sadducees, mentioned only here in Luke's Gospel, were a party closely tied to the priestly aristocracy. According to Josephus and the New Testament, they denied the resurrection of the dead and gave authority to the written Law of Moses rather than to the Pharisees' traditions.

The tax question was explosive. When Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, a census for taxation provoked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean, who taught that paying tribute to Caesar was disloyalty to God (Acts 5:37 mentions him). To say no to the tax was sedition; to say yes was to side with the occupier against many of the people. The denarius, a silver coin, carried the image of the emperor, in Jesus' day Tiberius, with an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus. Many Jews found such an image and claim offensive. By asking his questioners to produce the coin, Jesus showed that they were already carrying it.
cultural:
The parable of the tenants reflects a common arrangement in which an absentee landowner leased a vineyard to tenant farmers for a share of the harvest. Disputes over rents were familiar, and the tenants' reasoning that killing the heir would leave the vineyard to them shows how completely they have come to treat the owner's property as their own. Jesus' hearers would also have heard Isaiah 5, where Israel is the Lord's vineyard that produced bad fruit.

The Sadducees' question depends on levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). If a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow so that the dead man's name and inheritance would continue. The Sadducees built a deliberately absurd case, seven brothers and one wife, to make resurrection look ridiculous. The scribes' long robes, greetings in the marketplace, and best seats at synagogues and banquets were marks of honor in a culture where public status mattered greatly. Jesus' charge that they devour widows' houses may refer to exploiting widows' estates while acting as legal guardians or trustees, though the exact practice is uncertain.
literary: The chapter is a sequence of controversy stories, a form common in the Gospels, in which a question is put to Jesus, a trap is set, and his answer turns the trap back on the questioners. The first (verses 1 to 8) meets a question with a question. The second is a parable followed by Psalm 118:22, linking the rejected son with the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone. The third and fourth are trap questions, each ending with the questioners silenced (verses 26 and 40). Then Jesus becomes the questioner (verses 41 to 44), and finally he turns to warn his disciples in the hearing of the people. The word teacher runs through the chapter as Jesus' opponents address him, and the repeated notice that they feared the people shows the crowd as a protection they cannot yet get around.

outline.t: The parable of the wicked tenants

doctrines.note: Against the Sadducees, Jesus affirms the resurrection of the dead. Those raised will no longer die and are sons of God, sons of the resurrection. Resurrection life is not simply this life continued; it is transformed.

Jesus' question from Psalm 110 shows that the Messiah is more than a descendant of David. David calls him Lord. The parable of the tenants names him the owner's beloved son, distinct from all the servants (the prophets) sent before him.

Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. Earthly rulers have real but limited claims. The coin bears Caesar's image, and many interpreters have drawn the implied contrast: human beings bear God's image (Genesis 1:27), so the greater claim belongs to God.

words.note: Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. The leaders ask who gave Jesus authority to clear the temple and teach. His counter-question implies the answer: his authority, like John's, comes from heaven. Later in the chapter the spies hope to hand him over to the rule and authority of the governor, a different authority that will soon seem to hold him.

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up again. It refers to the dead being raised bodily at the end of the age, a hope developed in Daniel 12:2 and held by the Pharisees but rejected by the Sadducees. Jesus argues for it from the Torah itself, the part of Scripture the Sadducees held in highest regard.

Kephalē, head. Psalm 118:22 speaks of the stone the builders rejected becoming the head of the corner, the cornerstone or capstone that holds a building together. The early church used the verse again and again for Jesus (Acts 4:11, 1 Peter 2:7).

christ: Jesus reveals his own identity in this chapter more openly than before. In the parable, after many servants have been sent and abused, the owner sends his beloved son, a phrase that echoes the Father's voice at Jesus' baptism (3:22). The son is thrown out and killed, just as Jesus will be taken outside the city to die. The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, which the apostles will preach as the resurrection. And Jesus' question about Psalm 110 points to the answer the early church gave: the Messiah is both David's son by birth and David's Lord, seated at God's right hand. His argument for the resurrection from the burning bush, that God is the God of the living, prepares for his own rising.

hard.q: If there is no marriage in the resurrection, what happens to the love between husbands and wives?
hard.a: Jesus' answer can sound like a loss, especially to people in happy marriages. He is answering a specific question, though: whose legal wife will the widow be. Marriage in this age exists partly because people die; the levirate law the Sadducees cite was designed to carry a family name beyond death. In the age to come, where death is gone, that function ends. Jesus says the raised will be like the angels, not that they become angels, and only in this respect: they no longer die. He does not say that love or recognition ends. Many theologians have suggested that the exclusive covenant of marriage gives way to something fuller rather than less, and that the love learned in marriage is fulfilled in the marriage of Christ and his people, which the New Testament describes as the great wedding at the end of history. Scripture says little in detail about relationships in the resurrection, and readers should hold their conclusions with some restraint.

questions: Jesus says to give to God what is God's. If you bear God's image, what does that mean you owe him?
The leaders refused to answer honestly about John because they feared the consequences. When have you avoided the truth because the honest answer would cost you?
The scribes loved public honor. What forms does the desire for status take in religious communities today?
